schools.summary: Gill collects the rival figures for Samuel's age and answers the elders' use of it, experience having made him fitter for the office.
Henry accounts for the early decay by a childhood full of cares, holds that the years made him wiser and his dismissal unjust, and lays the sons' fall to the corrupting power of preferment.

Clarke denies the sons were judges in any proper sense and takes their iniquity apart into three charges; Wesley makes the office deputyship with appeal reserved, and holds that temptation only disclosed a corruption already there.

Ellicott dates Samuel's life from the capture of the ark, reads the sons' names as witnesses to their father's house, and follows the family down to Heman at David's court; Keil and Delitzsch set the three faults against the commands of the law.

debates.question: How old was Samuel when he made his sons judges?

sides.position: About sixty
Nearer seventy, reckoning from the capture of the ark and the recovery of the Philistines
The figures reported run from fifty-two to above seventy, and the text settles nothing

debates.question: Did office corrupt the sons or only expose them?

sides.position: Preferment and power spoiled men who had done well in subjection, and they discovered themselves once out of their father's sight
Opportunity and temptation created nothing, but disclosed what had been in them all along and hidden from Samuel

outliers.note: Alone in following the sons past their disgrace, holding that the punishment corrected them, since the family reappears in honour at David's court in Heman the grandson.

themes: when Samuel was old
they were judges in Beer-sheba
turned aside after lucre
took bribes, and perverted judgment
1.pericope_label: Samuel made his sons judges, and they turned aside after lucre

schools.summary: Gill identifies the elders as the heads of the tribes and refuses the plea of age as neither true reproach nor theirs to make.
Henry marks the orderly manner of the approach, calls the proposal new and surprising, answers both grievances, and reads the demand as a preference for pomp over a prophet's mantle.
Clarke makes a general in battle the point at which Israel principally aimed; Wesley holds their desires outran their reasons and that a king's sons would be as corrupt and less easily removed.

Keil and Delitzsch find the request framed on the law of the king and conclude the elders asked only what Moses had foretold; Ellicott treats the assembly as a standing institution and the plea as a compliment to Samuel.

debates.question: Was the elders' request itself unlawful?

sides.position: No, it asked no more than the law of the king had foretold and provided for
No, the resolution was perfectly justifiable, and the plea itself showed trust in their judge
Yes, it was an evil proposal that anticipated God's counsel for a king after his own heart
The request went further than their own reasons, and the grant aggravated the disease instead of curing it

outliers.note: Alone in reading the petition as a compliment, since to urge their judge's own infirmity and his children's unworthiness took confidence that he would do right against his own interest.

themes: all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together
thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways
make us a king to judge us
like all the nations
4.pericope_label: All the elders gathered to Ramah: make us a king to judge us

schools.summary: Gill rules out the personal provocations as the cause of the displeasure and takes the appeal to the exodus as proof that nothing new had happened.

Clarke calls the petition a formal renunciation of the divine government, has Samuel praying only to know God's mind, and turns on Grotius for grounding royal prerogative on the passage; Wesley adds pardon to the prayer and keeps prevention as the protest's aim.

Ellicott holds the request justified and the bitterness real, and expands the divine answer into a speech of tenderness and regret; Keil and Delitzsch fix the idiom of protesting as bearing witness against a person.

sides.position: To know God's mind in so weighty a business
Pardon for the people's sin first, and direction and help after it

debates.question: What does the order to protest solemnly require?

sides.position: To bear witness against them and point out their wrong, neither an earnest warning nor a solemn expounding
To inform them what they were asking, so that they might consider whether to persist
To prevent the sin and the misery, if prevention were still possible

outliers.note: Alone in reading the transaction as a deliberate lowering of God's first intention for Israel, with the veil lifted on what he ventures to call the Creator's sorrowful regret.

themes: the thing displeased Samuel
they have not rejected thee, but me
according to all the works which they have done
protest solemnly unto them
6.pericope_label: They have not rejected thee, but me; protest solemnly unto them

schools.summary: Gill fixes the word rendered manner as what kings will do rather than ought, and brings Aristotle's absolute kingdom against the request.
Henry distinguishes the law of God from the manner of men as two different measures, and ends on the hard masters that world and flesh prove.

Keil and Delitzsch construe the sons' service word by word and defend the singular suffix against emendation; Ellicott puts the speech as a question whether Israel would trade a republic for a despotism, and sketches the court life that would follow.
Wesley reads the taking as done injuriously and by violence for the king's own glory, and weighs the loss of the daughters as the heavier grief.

debates.question: What does the manner of the king describe?

sides.position: Not the course a king ought to take but the course kings in general will take, being inclined to arbitrary power
The king's right as proclaimed, to be construed clause by clause
A question put to the people, whether they would exchange their republic for a despotism
Taking by violence, for the king's own fancy and glory rather than the kingdom's necessity

outliers.note: Alone in reaching outside scripture for a philosopher's definition, setting Aristotle's absolute kingdom against theocracy and his rule that whoever would have a man reign brings in a man's appetite.

themes: this will be the manner of the king
he will take your sons
captains over thousands, and captains over fifties
your daughters to be confectionaries
10.pericope_label: This will be the manner of the king: he will take your sons

schools.summary: Gill restricts the threat to the increase of the land, arguing from Naboth's vineyard that kings could not take freeholds by absolute authority, and extends the tenth of the flocks to the herds.

Keil and Delitzsch take the best possessions as forfeit, emend the goodliest young men to oxen on the Greek, and defend the passage against a late date; Ellicott reaches the same emendation independently and traces the forecast through the northern kingdom to the captivity.
Wesley has fields taken by fraud or force as Ahab took Naboth's, keeps the literal eunuchs as a further charge, and reads the unanswered cry as returning their own deafness.

debates.question: Could the king take the land itself, or only what it yielded?

sides.position: Only the increase, since Ahab could not simply seize Naboth's vineyard and Jezebel had to contrive it
The possessions themselves, by fraud or force, and given away to his servants

debates.question: What does the word rendered officers mean here?

sides.position: Royal chamberlains, the literal eunuch taken in a wider sense
Literal eunuchs, so that the king would unman his own people against the command of God

outliers.note: Alone in carrying the forecast down through the history, the yoke felt under Solomon, the kingdom split at his death, and no prayers availing under the northern dynasties until the captivity.

themes: he will take your fields, and your vineyards
the tenth of your seed
ye shall be his servants
the Lord will not hear you in that day
14.pericope_label: He will take the tenth of your seed, and ye shall cry out

schools.summary: Gill calls the refusal stupidity and makes unlikeness to other nations the people's lost honour and happiness.
Clarke reads off the three clauses as rejecting Samuel, demanding a head of state and a general of the armies; Wesley answers the military plea from the battle lately won by prayer and thunder.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that the description of the king's right should have brought the elders to reflection; Ellicott has the warning debated in formal assembly and the first request reaffirmed by a majority.

debates.question: How should the people's refusal be characterised?

sides.position: Obstinacy that took the king and his manner together in defiance of a solemn warning
A decision reached after careful debate in a formal assembly and held to by a majority

outliers.note: Alone in giving the refusal a procedure, the prophet's words weighed in a formal council and the original terms deliberately reaffirmed rather than shouted down.

themes: the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel
we will have a king over us
that we also may be like all the nations
go out before us, and fight our battles
19.pericope_label: Nay, but we will have a king over us, like all the nations

schools.summary: Gill has Samuel hear the people out in silence and answer nothing, and leaves the manner of the divine reply open between a voice and an impulse on the mind.

Clarke places the rehearsing at the altar and then sets out the whole affair in numbered propositions on government; Wesley makes the private repetition serve for vindication and as the ground of prayer.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the unspoken condition of the dismissal; Ellicott locates the prayer at Samuel's own sanctuary, counts this the third time the same word was given, and reads the dismissal as proof that the elders were a representative body.

debates.question: Where and why did Samuel rehearse the people's words?

sides.position: At the altar, laying the whole business before God in secret devotion
At the sanctuary he had set up in his own Ramah, pouring out his heart there
Privately, for his own vindication and comfort and as the ground of his prayer
In silence, giving the people no answer and reporting the matter instead

outliers.note: Alone in turning the dismissal into ten numbered propositions on government, holding that God never resigned the supreme rule and that no king of Judah made new laws, then defending the mixed British constitution at length and closing on the weight of taxes.

themes: he rehearsed them in the ears of the Lord
hearken unto their voice, and make them a king
go ye every man unto his city
21.pericope_label: Samuel rehearsed it in the ears of the Lord: hearken unto their voice
